title: The shortest psalm (Psalm 116 [117])
hook: two verses: praise the Lord, all nations

segments.voice: Yesterday, from the rising of the sun: the God who stoops down to lift the poor out of the dust. Your line was he raises the needy. Whose spirits did you lift? Day one hundred eighty-one.

Some psalms go on for pages. Some take ten minutes to pray. And then there's this one. You could say it while the kettle boils. You could say it in the time it takes a traffic light to change. Two verses. Barely thirty words in English. It's the shortest psalm in the whole Psalter, and it's often called the shortest chapter in the entire Bible. And yet in those thirty words it manages to invite the whole planet. Not one people, not one city, not one church. Everyone. Today: the shortest psalm.
screen: `SOME PSALMS RUN FOR PAGES.` → `THIS ONE: TWO VERSES.` → `AND IT INVITES EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here is the whole thing, in the Douay-Rheims: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people. For his mercy is confirmed upon us: and the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever." That's it. That's the psalm. Look at the shape. The first verse is the invitation, and it's as wide as it can be: all nations, all peoples. The second verse gives the reason, and it's two old Hebrew words that run all through the Psalms. Mercy is chesed, the steady, loyal love that keeps a promise. Truth is emet, faithfulness, the thing you can lean your weight on. So the reason the whole world is invited to praise is simple: God's love holds, and God's faithfulness lasts. Second, where it sits. In Jewish worship this psalm belongs to the Hallel, the psalms of praise sung at Passover and the great feasts, and Jews still sing it today. Many scholars think the hymn Jesus and his friends sang after the Last Supper was part of the Hallel. Third, who picked it up. Saint Paul quotes this psalm in his letter to the Romans, to say the good news was meant for the nations, not one people alone. And the Church kept singing it in Latin, Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes. Mozart set it to music. Pilgrims at Taizé sing it over and over. So the shortest psalm turns out to have one of the longest reaches. A Catholic can pray it at Vespers, a Jewish family sings it at Passover, and both are singing the same two verses about everyone.
screen: `TWO VERSES: THE INVITE AND THE REASON.` · `MERCY AND TRUTH: LOVE THAT HOLDS.` · `SUNG AT PASSOVER, THEN AND NOW.` · `PAUL, MOZART, TAIZÉ: ALL NATIONS.` · then, large: `O PRAISE THE LORD, ALL YE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the shortest psalm, three times. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the two verses slowly, once. Then again, and this time picture one place far from you, a country you've never visited, people waking up there right now. Then a third time, and picture someone near you who is nothing like you. If you don't pray, just hold those three pictures in the quiet: here, far away, and next door. The bell holds the time.
The shortest psalm. Psalm one hundred sixteen in the Catholic numbering, one hundred seventeen in the Hebrew. Two verses that invite all nations. Today's word.
Your line: all nations. Today, when you see a face or hear an accent from somewhere far away, remember the psalm had room for them before you ever met them. Day one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 116 [117] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and it is often sung in Latin as Laudate Dominum; some pray it through the day as a short prayer of praise.

what it means: two verses that invite the whole world to praise, because God's love holds and his faithfulness lasts.
what a scholar hears: chesed and emet, the covenant pair, and a psalm from the Passover Hallel that Paul quotes in Romans 15.

notes: Douay-Rheims text of Psalm 116 given from memory; confirm wording and punctuation.
'Often called the shortest chapter in the Bible': a common claim; confirm, and confirm 'barely thirty words in English'.

Psalm 117 as part of the Egyptian Hallel (Psalms 113–118) sung at Passover and festivals; the hymn after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26) as probably the Hallel is a common scholarly view, stated as 'many scholars think'.
Mozart's Laudate Dominum is from the Vesperae solennes de confessore (K. 339); the Taizé chant 'Laudate Dominum' is also well known. Confirm.
chesed/emet glosses as 'mercy'/'truth' in Douay-Rheims; confirm the Hebrew words behind this psalm's verse 2.
